newsitem.title: USA: U.S. MUNICIPALS - PRICES FIRM THOUGH RETAIL ABSENT.
newsitem.headline: U.S. MUNICIPALS - PRICES FIRM THOUGH RETAIL ABSENT.

text.p: U.S. municipal bonds firmed slightly early Thursday, even though weekly jobless claims showed a bit more strength than predicted, as most new issues seemed to be do fairly well despite the lack of retail demand.

Estimating bids rose around 0.01, a trader said "We're surprised retail isn't back, they haven't come back although we had a back-up in yields. I don't know if all the July reinvestment money already is gone, or if all the money is going to the equities market."
Individual investors also might be more focused on vacations in August, he added.
Nassau County, N.Y., sold $110 million of improvement bonds, which were priced with a 5.07 percent yield in 2013.
Refunding bonds sold Tuesday by the New York City Water Finance Authority were trading at net, a trader said.
"You got the new issues probably placed pretty well," a trader said, noting Georgia's $240 million general obligations, also priced Tuesday, sold out swiftly.

In contrast, the New York City Water Finance Authority was forced to trim the refunding to about $288 million from as much as $365 million due to the market's just over two-point drop last Friday, and the sale only attracted $12 million of retail orders in a presale period.

Pittsburgh Airport's $464 million of refunding bonds only drew $15 million of retail buyers, and were priced during the presale period with a top yield of 5.53 percent in 2016. The issue priced the offering for institutional investors at a top yield of 5.53 percent in 2016, slight trimming the size to $453 million.

Georgia's bonds were unusually attractive because they are noncallable and are a quality credit, but Pittsburgh Airport's sale might have a more difficult time because some of the debt is subject to the alternative minimum tax. Also, airport bonds are sold much more frequently.

The latest weekly jobless claims rose to 300,000 in the week ending August 2, below the average forecast for a 307,000 reading. The previous claims were revised to 275,000 from 277,000. The market also was looking ahead to the Treasury's auction of $10 billion of 30-year bonds at 1300 EDT.

The Standard and Poor's Corp Blue List, the main yardstick for the secondary market, stood at $1.4 billion, and traders noted that potential buyers, as they have for the past six months or so, continued to sell outstanding bonds to make room for new issues.
Municipal bond sales on Thursday were expected to total $530 million in 23 sales, according to Reuters Municipal Bond Information Group.
Negotiated offerings totalled $420 million in 10 sales, with a $150 million Ohio Housing Financing Authority offering through Goldman, Sachs & Co. topping the list.
On the competitive side, 13 sales totaling $110 million were scheduled. A $40 million Monmouth County, N.J., offering at 1100 EDT was the largest.
In the secondary market, Dade County, Florida, Water & Sewer Systems Revenues of 2021, which pay a 5-1/4 percent coupon, were offered at 5.38 percent NET, unchanged.
Municipal Electricity Authority, Georgia, bonds of 2026, which pay a five percent coupon, were offered at 5.35 percent, NET.
